title: THE FIRST FRAME
goal: Catch the first thought before it expands into a whole story.
steps:
1. Trigger — A trigger flickers.
2. Pause Story — Do not explain it yet.
3. Capture Thought — Pin the first thought, picture, or prediction exactly as it arrived.
4. Quote — Put quotation marks around it.
5. Close Capture — The catch ends there; no life story, no courtroom, no spiral.
win: The trigger was captured exactly once without becoming a life story, trial, or spiral.
supports:
• Test the assumption; delay major conclusions when upset.
• Separate possibility from probability; ask what would change your mind.
• Avoid treating guesses as facts; notice absolute words like always.
• Separate guess from evidence; check another angle.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; check what you actually know.
formula_flow: Trigger → Pause Story → Capture Thought → Quote → Close Capture
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if holding the thought in mind makes you feel less steady or more upset.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE TWO-TRAY TEST
goal: Weigh visible facts on both sides before deciding what they mean.
steps:
1. Imagine Trays — Imagine two trays.
2. Name Sides — Name the left SUPPORTS IT and the right DOESN’T FIT.
3. Sort Facts — Drop only visible facts into them—no feelings disguised as evidence.
4. Switch Sides — Now cover the fuller tray and read the neglected one silently.
5. Balance Verdict — Finish with a verdict that can hold both sides without pretending they weigh the same.
win: Your verdict included supporting evidence and the facts your feeling had been overlooking.
supports:
• Eat, drink, or rest if needed; notice what changed physically.
• Do one steadying action; lower nearby noise.
• Name the feeling plainly; check the facts separately.
• Slow physical pace; give the feeling time to move.
• Check basic needs; name the emotion.
formula_flow: Imagine Trays → Name Sides → Sort Facts → Switch Sides → Balance Verdict
safety:
PAUSE
Stop when you are recycling arguments instead of discovering evidence.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WORST CASE, WITH EXITS
goal: Turn the feared ending into a realistic path through and beyond it.
steps:
1. Name Fear — Picture the feared ending in one line.
2. Build Exits — Under it build four rungs: WHAT HAPPENS; WHAT I DO NEXT; WHO OR WHAT HELPS; HOW RECOVERY COULD BEGIN.
3. Add Likely — Add a fifth rung for the outcome that is actually most likely.
4. Climb Route — Move through the five steps once in your mind.
5. Act Now — Then take the first coping action available now.
win: The worst case gained exits, support, recovery steps, and a more likely outcome before you acted.
supports:
• Question absolute words; check what you actually know.
• Test the assumption; check the whole situation.
• Check the base rate; use recent, concrete evidence.
• Ask what would change your mind; use current facts.
• Check another angle; delay the verdict.
formula_flow: Name Fear → Build Exits → Add Likely → Climb Route → Act Now
safety:
PAUSE
Do not run this alone for immediate danger, medical crisis, or trauma flooding.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE GREY DIAL
goal: Find the evidence-based middle between two extreme verdicts.
steps:
1. Name Extremes — Name the two extremes your mind is using.
2. Build Scale — Build a 0–10 scale between them and say three real anchor points: 2, 5, and 8.
3. Place Today — Place today’s event where the evidence fits—not where the emotion shouts.
4. Choose Response — Choose a response matched to that exact setting.
win: The event landed at a specific point on the scale and your response matched that setting.
supports:
• Use recent, concrete evidence; check the whole situation.
• Test the assumption; separate guess from evidence.
• Ask what else could fit; question absolute words.
• Check the base rate; notice absolute words like always.
• Use current facts; delay the verdict.
formula_flow: Name Extremes → Build Scale → Place Today → Choose Response
safety:
PAUSE

This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: BORROW THEIR MIRROR
goal: Judge yourself by the same evidence standard you would use for someone you trust.
steps:
1. Imagine Trusted — Imagine a trusted person bringing you the same facts.

title: THE RULE UNDER THE RULE
goal: Find the hidden rule beneath a painful thought without automatically obeying it.
steps:
1. Picture Painful — Picture the painful thought.
2. Ask Meaning — Ask, ‘If that were true, what would it mean about me, others, or life?’ Answer quickly, then ask the same question of the answer.
3. Continue Stable — Continue only until one stable rule repeats.
4. Box Rule — Put that rule in a mental box.
5. Apply Today — Today’s task is to inspect it, not obey it.
win: A repeating rule became visible and stayed boxed as something to inspect rather than follow.
supports:
• Stop planning after one action; begin while unsure.
• Open only what you need; make it visible.
• Begin with the easiest part; restart quickly.
• Use two minutes; choose a rough beginning.
• Reward starting, not finishing; start with one minute.
formula_flow: Picture Painful → Ask Meaning → Continue Stable → Box Rule → Apply Today
safety:
PAUSE
Stop descent if it triggers feeling unreal or disconnected, hopelessness, or overwhelming material.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE OLD-RULE CONTRABAND FILE
goal: Keep one real exception that your negative self-story usually throws away.
steps:
1. Capture — Catch one event your negative self-story would normally delete.
2. Describe Happened — Say what happened, why it really does not fit the old rule, and which convenient excuse the rule will use to dismiss it.
3. Seal — Seal the entry in your mind as usable evidence and bring it back tomorrow once—no chanting.
win: A fact that contradicted the old rule stayed recorded even after you noticed its usual excuse.
supports:
• Add the missing context; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Use a real example; separate guess from evidence.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; check another angle.
• Delay major conclusions when upset; check what you actually know.
• Notice absolute words like always; separate possibility from probability.
formula_flow: Capture → Describe Happened → Seal
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use exceptions to deny real problems that need action.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE FORECAST SCOREBOARD
goal: Track how confident predictions compare with what actually happens over time.
steps:
1. Count Hit — Before an uncertain event, remember four items: prediction, confidence %, deadline, and what counts as a hit.
2. Keep Result — Afterward, hold the result without rewriting the original entry.
3. Calculate — Calculate the gap between confidence and reality.
4. Spot the Bias — After five rounds, look for your recurring bias.
win: The original forecast stayed intact long enough to reveal the gap between confidence and reality.
supports:
• Stop planning after one action; begin with the easiest part.
• Set a two-minute timer; remove one barrier.
• Restart quickly; touch the first item.
• Lower standards briefly; prepare first.
• Choose a rough beginning; prepare the task in advance.
formula_flow: Count Hit → Keep Result → Calculate → Spot the Bias
safety:
PAUSE
Retire the ledger if it feeds compulsive monitoring.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE SKY DOES NOT BECOME THE WEATHER
goal: Notice thoughts, feelings, and roles without shrinking yourself to any of them.
steps:
1. Name Thought — Name one thought, one feeling, and one role active now.
2. Say Being — For each, say: ‘This is being noticed.’ Search for the noticing itself—its colour, age, or mood.
3. Rest Openness — If none can be found, rest with that openness for ten seconds.
4. Land in Feet — Return by feeling both feet.
win: Each experience became something being noticed rather than the whole person noticing it.
supports:
• Choose one value-led action; act before motivation.
• Choose aligned action; check whose goal.
• Review what the action costs; remove one conflicting commitment.
• Name what matters today; review the cost.
• Pick one value for this decision; use one priority.

title: TRANSLATE THE VERDICT
goal: Break a harsh judgment into facts, preference, and likely consequence.
steps:
1. Take Judgement — Take one judgement and mentally translate it into three components: visible facts, personal preference, likely consequence.
2. Prefer Decision — Example: ‘Awful meeting’ becomes ‘Two interruptions; I prefer turn-taking; the decision stayed unclear.’ Respond to the components rather than fighting the label.
win: The label stopped being one solid verdict and became separate pieces you could respond to.
supports:
• Interrupt the usual sequence; keep replacement easy.
• Interrupt the sequence; reduce easy access to triggers.
• Make the old habit harder; reset without self-criticism.
• Use the same replacement repeatedly; move the cue.
• Change the environment; add small friction.
formula_flow: Take Judgement → Prefer Decision
safety:
PAUSE
Keep moral language where clear ethical wrongdoing must be named.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

win: One safe option carried you through the interval and you reassessed afterward.

• Ship useful work; make the rough version first.
• Set finish time; separate important errors from polish.

title: UPGRADE THE WAITING ROOM
goal: Improve one part of a hard waiting period without pretending the reason is okay.
steps:
1. Pick Best — Choose one lever now: picture support, connect to meaning, offer a brief prayer, relax one area, or do one thing fully.
2. Use Lever — Use only one lever until the interval ends.
3. Upgrade the Minute — You are improving the room, not denying why you are there.
win: One chosen lever made the interval more livable while the underlying situation stayed acknowledged.
supports:
• Keep movements gentle; reduce caffeine.
• Loosen your shoulders; avoid symptom searching.
• Give the surge time to pass; use ordinary surroundings.
• Unclench your jaw; keep your body supported.
• Look at ordinary objects nearby; reduce extra stimulation.
formula_flow: Pick Best → Use Lever → Upgrade the Minute
safety:
PAUSE
Move from coping to problem-solving when the situation requires direct action.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: DOES THE FEELING FIT THE FILE?
goal: Check whether the feeling's intensity matches the verified present threat.
steps:
1. Imagine Four Lanes — Picture four lanes: event, meaning, verified evidence, present threat.
2. Compare Emotion — Compare the emotion’s intensity with the present-threat lane.
3. Use Feeling — If they fit, use the feeling’s message.
4. Update Meaning — If they exceed it, regulate first and revise the meaning.
win: You either used the emotion's message or regulated first because the facts did not support its volume.
supports:
• Use plain language; do one steadying action.
• Slow physical pace; check basic needs.
• Name the feeling plainly; eat, drink, or rest if needed.
• Check the facts separately; use simple words for the problem.
• Separate feeling from fact; lower stimulation for a minute.
formula_flow: Imagine Four Lanes → Compare Emotion → Use Feeling → Update Meaning
safety:
PAUSE
Trust immediate protective action when evidence shows real threat.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: LET THE EMOTION FINISH ONE CHAPTER
goal: Let the current emotional chapter finish before jumping into the next one.
steps:
1. Identify Chapter — Spot the current chapter only: sensation, meaning, action urge, or settling.
2. Permit — Permit the next natural chapter while withholding later ones.
3. Pause Meaning — If sensation is active, do not interpret; if meaning is clear, do not act yet.
4. Continue Genuine — Continue until a genuine settling marker—breath change, warmth, tears ending, posture release—appears.
win: A real settling marker appeared without sensation, meaning, and action being rushed together.
supports:
• Change locations; make access harder.
• Eat if hungry; ride the peak.
• Make access less convenient; avoid bargaining with the urge.
• Leave the trigger; change rooms if possible.
• Tell someone early; avoid bargaining.
formula_flow: Identify Chapter → Permit → Pause Meaning → Continue Genuine
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if the process floods awareness or removes action control.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

2. Find Practical Resource — Identify one practical resource available today.
3. Choose Helpful Place — Choose a familiar place that supports present-time orientation.
4. Use Current Strength — Name a current skill you can use without recalling trauma detail.
5. Plan Contact Time — Set a specific time to contact support if needed.

A person, resource, place, current skill, and contact time were all available in present-day terms.

• Contact someone trusted; use familiar surroundings.
• Name the place; move gently.
• Name today's date; hold a familiar object.

• Contact someone you trust; feel your feet.

PAUSE
Keep your eyes open. Use only present-day room, date, place and support orientation. Do not revisit memories in detail, use trauma imagery, intensify sensations, or attempt unsupervised processing. Stop for flooding, dissociation, or weakened orientation and connect with qualified human support.
This is stabilisation only, not trauma treatment.

title: STAMP WHERE THE DETAIL CAME FROM
goal: Rate a memory detail by where it came from, not by how intense it feels.
steps:
1. Pick Detail — Choose one small memory detail; do not mentally revisit the event in detail.

3. Rate Confidence — Give the detail a confidence word—high, medium, low, or unknown—based on its source rather than its emotional intensity.
4. Keep Core — Picture one core fact that remains reliable and let the other detail keep its honest uncertainty.
win: The detail received a source label and honest confidence while one reliable core fact stayed separate.
supports:
• Name what is unknown; notice when checking stops helping.
• Use a deadline; delay reassurance.
• Limit checking; name what is known.
• Accept a small margin of risk; leave one question unanswered.
• Stop reopening choices; use a decision deadline.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not force missing details; stop and seek support if the memory becomes overwhelming or disorienting.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: OCEAN IN THE THROAT
goal: Make the breath softly audible, then soften effort until the sound nearly disappears.
steps:
1. Create Soft — Narrow the throat only enough to create a soft ocean texture, never a rasp.
2. Let Sound — Let that sound accompany an easy inhale and exhale.
3. Reduce Effort — Reduce effort until someone beside you might barely hear it.
4. Release Technique — After several waves, release the technique completely.
win: The ocean-like texture stayed gentle and was fully released after a few easy waves.
supports:
• Unclench your jaw and shoulders; avoid repeated pulse checking.
• Stay somewhere physically safe; seek care for new severe symptoms.
• Let breaths happen; sit somewhere safe.
• Reduce caffeine; wait out the surge.
• Keep movements gentle; unclench your jaw.
formula_flow: Create Soft → Let Sound → Reduce Effort → Release Technique
safety:
PAUSE
Do not practise through irritation, constriction, breathing illness, or dizziness.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: INSTALL THE COUNTER-QUALITY
goal: Give the opposite quality a believable thought, posture, and action.
steps:
1. Name Active — Name the active pattern and the wholesome quality opposite with it: cruelty/kindness, panic/steadiness, greed/sufficiency.
2. Act Counter — Produce one thought, posture, and act expressing the counter-quality.
3. Keep Credible — Keep it credible rather than grand.
4. Train — Train the opposite channel through embodiment.
win: The counter-quality showed up in all three channels without needing to feel grand.
supports:
• Sit somewhere safe; reduce extra stimulation.
• Avoid repeated pulse checking; let breathing stay natural.
• Wait out the surge; avoid symptom searching.
• Stop body scanning; keep movements gentle.
• Let breaths happen; unclench your jaw and shoulders.

safety:
PAUSE
Countering must not suppress valid grief, anger, or protective fear.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ERASE THE OBJECT, KEEP THE CONTACT
goal: Let an imagined object lose its labels and shape while attention itself remains.
steps:
1. Stabilise — Stabilise attention on one simple imagined form.
2. Remove Name — Gradually remove its name, meaning, shape, and boundary in that order.
3. Attend Contact — Preserve the sense of attending as the form loses definition.
4. Rest Briefly — Rest with contact that no longer depends on a clear thing.
win: Name, meaning, form, and boundary faded in sequence without the act of attending disappearing.
supports:
• Use one clear sentence; keep the limit simple.
• Do not overexplain the limit; state consequences clearly.
• Repeat the same wording calmly; leave reactions with them.
• Keep consequences realistic; notice resentment as a warning.
• Decide your limit before answering; let guilt pass.
formula_flow: Stabilise → Remove Name → Attend Contact → Rest Briefly
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid object dissolution when prone to derealisation or perceptual instability.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

PLAY TIME
about 1 minute

GOAL
Let an imagined object lose its labels and shape while attention itself remains.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Stabilise — Stabilise attention on one simple imagined form.
2. Remove Name — Gradually remove its name, meaning, shape, and boundary in that order.
3. Attend Contact — Preserve the sense of attending as the form loses definition.
4. Rest Briefly — Rest with contact that no longer depends on a clear thing.

WIN
Name, meaning, form, and boundary faded in sequence without the act of attending disappearing.

• Use one clear sentence; keep the limit simple.
• Do not overexplain the limit; state consequences clearly.
• Repeat the same wording calmly; leave reactions with them.
• Keep consequences realistic; notice resentment as a warning.
• Decide your limit before answering; let guilt pass.

MIND BEND
Attention can remain when the object becomes unclear, suggesting that contact and concept are not the same thing.

FORMULA FLOW
Stabilise → Remove Name → Attend Contact → Rest Briefly

title: THE FIVE-LAYER INSPECTION
goal: Check body, energy, mind, judgment, and ease before deciding which layer needs action.
steps:
1. Move Body — Move through body, energy, mind, intellect, and deep ease.
2. Ask Change — At each layer ask what is present, what changes, and how it is known.
3. Keep All Layers — Do not discard any layer.
4. Place Like — Place them like translucent sheets within awareness, then select the layer needed for practical action.
win: Several layers stayed visible at once, and the practical response was chosen from the one that mattered now.
supports:
• Slow physical pace; separate feeling from fact.
• Delay the message; avoid decisions at peak emotion.
• Wait before sending messages; lower nearby noise.
• Notice body tension; name the feeling plainly.
• Name the emotion; do one steadying action.
formula_flow: Move Body → Ask Change → Keep All Layers → Place Like
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid abstract layer work when immediate grounding is needed.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE WAKING DREAM CHECK
goal: Separate the raw facts of an event from the connections your mind constructed around them.
steps:
1. Take Event — Take one rigid reading of an event.
2. Compare Dream — Compare it with a dream: both organise fragments into a convincing world.
3. Identify Facts — Spot which facts are raw and which connections were constructed.
4. Try Construction — Try one alternate construction and observe how lived experience changes.
win: One alternate interpretation changed lived experience without requiring the original facts to change.
supports:
• Stop checking their numbers; use your own priorities.
• Choose your own measure; do one action for your life.
• Notice what you cannot see; check your own progress.
• Compare with your past self; track progress by your values.
• Keep context visible; limit social media exposure.
formula_flow: Take Event → Compare Dream → Identify Facts → Try Construction
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid dreamlike framing if it increases derealisation or psychotic symptoms.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: RETURN THE PROJECTION TO SENDER
goal: Separate the evidence about someone else from the fear or rule you may be projecting onto it.
steps:
1. Picture Quality — Picture the quality you are assigning outward.
2. Ask Internal — Ask what internal expectation, fear, or rule would make that quality especially visible.
3. Name External — Name the external evidence separately.
4. Keep Facts — Keep what the facts support; return the excess meaning to your own inquiry.
win: External facts kept their weight while unsupported extra meaning returned to your own inquiry.
supports:
• Interrupt the sequence; change the environment.
• Add small friction; reset without self-criticism.
• Use the same replacement repeatedly; notice the trigger.
• Replace one response; keep replacement easy.
• Make the new habit easier; interrupt the usual sequence.

safety:
PAUSE

This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

steps:

title: BOX THE PROBLEM
goal: Shrink a vague problem into its current state, desired state, and measurable gap.
steps:
1. Picture Lines — Picture three lines: CURRENT CONDITION; DESIRED CONDITION; MEASURABLE GAP.
2. Remove History — Remove history unless it changes the gap.
3. Give Problem — Give the problem a time horizon and one owner.
4. Statement — If the statement still contains ‘everything,’ shrink it again.
win: History and 'everything' fell away, leaving a bounded gap with a time horizon and owner.
supports:
• Expect slips and restart quickly; change the environment first.
• Change one cue; reset without self-criticism.
• Reduce easy access to triggers; notice the first automatic moment.
• Change the environment; delay the routine.
• Add small friction; make the new habit easier.
formula_flow: Picture Lines → Remove History → Give Problem → Statement
safety:
PAUSE
Some pain needs witnessing rather than conversion into a problem.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FIXED, FLEXIBLE, UNKNOWN, ASSUMED
goal: Sort each barrier by what can be accepted, changed, checked, or tested.
steps:
1. Name — Name every barrier.
2. Mark Category — Mark each barrier as fixed, flexible, unknown, or assumed.
3. Test Assumed — Accept the fixed, negotiate the flexible, investigate the unknown, and test the assumed.
4. Start What Moves — Begin with the highest-impact item whose category permits movement.
win: Every obstacle received a category, and the highest-impact movable one became the starting point.
supports:
• Decide your limit before answering; use a short no.
• Notice resentment as a warning; take time before saying yes.
• Notice resentment early; let guilt pass.
• Delay your answer; leave their reaction with them.
• Repeat without arguing; use one clear sentence.
formula_flow: Name → Mark Category → Test Assumed → Start What Moves
safety:
PAUSE
Reclassify when new evidence changes a limit’s status.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE NO-JUDGEMENT OPTION STORM
goal: Create five genuinely different options before judging whether any of them will work.
steps:
1. Open Possibilities — Generate five options without ranking, explaining, or defending them.
2. Vary Them — Include one conventional, one tiny, one reversible, one collaborative, and one unusual safe option.
3. Delay Judgement — Only after all five exist may feasibility enter the room.
win: Conventional, tiny, reversible, collaborative, and unusual possibilities all existed before feasibility entered.
supports:
• Interrupt the sequence; expect slips and restart quickly.
• Notice the trigger; keep replacement easy.
• Interrupt the usual sequence; add small friction.
• Reduce easy access to triggers; make the new habit easier.
• Reset without self-criticism; notice the first automatic moment.

safety:

title: THE AFTERSHOCK CLOCK
goal: Give post-event activation a recovery window before letting it rewrite what the event meant.
steps:
1. Set Reasonable — Set a reasonable after-event window during which shakiness, mental loops, fatigue, or emotion are expected echoes.
2. Picture Time — Picture its end time.
3. Notice Sensations — Until then, keep sensations but forbid them from changing your meaning of what happened.
4. Reassess — Reassess after recovery and sleep where possible.
win: Shakiness, fatigue, or looping were treated as echoes until the chosen reassessment point rather than fresh evidence.
supports:
• Keep movements gentle; seek care for new severe symptoms.
• Unclench your jaw; let breathing stay natural.
• Keep your body supported; wait out the surge.
• Reduce caffeine; sip water if it helps.
• Stop body scanning; unclench your jaw and shoulders.
formula_flow: Set Reasonable → Picture Time → Notice Sensations → Reassess
safety:
PAUSE
Seek care when symptoms are severe, worsening, or medically concerning.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: LET THE IMAGE FIND ITS LAST FRAME
goal: Let a troubling image reach its own final frame without adding verbal commentary.
steps:
1. Bring Image — Bring up the image gently and prohibit verbal commentary.
2. Allow Move — Allow it to move at its own speed until it reaches a stable frame or natural ending.
3. Check Your Position — Notice whether your position, distance, or available action changes.
4. Use Sensory — Reorient afterward using present sensory facts.
win: The image moved to a stable ending and your present sensory surroundings were restored afterward.
supports:
• Keep eyes open; touch a stable surface.
• Feel your feet; look around the room.
• Notice temperature and texture; feel both feet.
• Feel the chair; notice room temperature.
• Name three visible objects; keep your eyes on something steady.
formula_flow: Bring Image → Allow Move → Check Your Position → Use Sensory
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use alone with traumatic imagery, hallucinations, or destabilisation.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CAPTURE THE MODEL’S MISS
goal: Preserve the original prediction when reality surprises it.
steps:
1. Keep Both Versions — The moment an outcome differs from expectation, keep both versions verbatim.
2. State Size — State the size and direction of the error.
3. Name Miss — Finish with: ‘The old model must now explain…’ and name the discrepancy.
4. Preserve Forecast — Do not let hindsight rewrite the original prediction.
win: The expected outcome and the actual outcome stayed side by side, forcing the old model to account for its miss.
supports:
• Check the base rate; delay the verdict.
• Question absolute words; use current facts.
• Add the missing context; separate guess from evidence.
• Notice absolute words like always; delay major conclusions when upset.
• Look for one missing fact; use recent, concrete evidence.
formula_flow: Keep Both Versions → State Size → Name Miss → Preserve Forecast
safety:
PAUSE
Do not overlearn from one noisy or unrepresentative result.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

goal: Keep felt certainty on a different meter from the quality of the evidence.

title: SAME FACTS, THREE ASSUMPTIONS
goal: Run the same facts through different assumptions and look for the action that survives them.
steps:
1. Keep Observations — Keep all observations fixed.
2. Reframe Three Ways — Run the same facts through three different assumptions about motive, capability, or context.
3. Identify Action — For each, spot the one simple action it recommends.
4. Compare Action — Compare which action remains robust across versions.
win: Three interpretations produced three recommendations, making the robust action easier to see without settling motive first.
supports:
• Ask what would disprove it; separate guess from evidence.
• Check the whole situation; separate possibility from probability.
• Delay major conclusions when upset; use a real example.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; question absolute words.
• Test the assumption; notice absolute words like always.
formula_flow: Keep Observations → Reframe Three Ways → Identify Action → Compare Action
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid invented alternatives that contradict established evidence.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FORECAST WITH A LANDING ZONE
goal: Forecast a reasonable range and learn from where reality lands inside or outside it.
steps:
1. Predict Range — Predict a range rather than a perfect point.
2. State Acceptable — State the acceptable error band and why it is reasonable.
3. Measure Reality — After the result, measure reality check: inside, near, or outside the band.
4. Widen the Landing — Adjust future range width instead of declaring success or failure.
win: The result was scored against an error band, then the next range changed instead of your worth being graded.
supports:
• Ask what is actually required; define good enough first.
• Ship useful work; compare against the brief.
• Leave minor flaws; separate errors from polish.
• Limit checking; use actual requirements.
• Stop low-value changes; set finish time.
formula_flow: Predict Range → State Acceptable → Measure Reality → Widen the Landing
safety:
PAUSE
Keep tight limits where safety or engineering precision requires them.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WAIT FOR THE EVIDENCE THAT CAN EXIST
goal: Wait only for future information that can genuinely change the choice.
steps:
1. Name Future — Name the future information that could really change the choice, when it becomes available, and how each possible result would alter action.
2. Wait Evidence — Wait only for that evidence.
3. Reject Delay — Everything else is delay wearing a research badge.
win: The needed evidence, arrival time, and action consequence were defined, leaving unrelated research without a reason to continue.
supports:
• Cut the task; use two minutes.
• Lower standards briefly; make the first move tiny.
• Restart quickly; shrink the first action.
• Use a visible cue; lower the quality bar.
• Make it visible; start before you feel ready.
formula_flow: Name Future → Wait Evidence → Reject Delay
safety:
PAUSE
Act with current information if delay itself creates material risk.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FIND THE MOVE NO FEELING MUST BETRAY
goal: Choose an action that crosses none of your emotions' reasonable red lines.
steps:
1. Seat Feelings — Label up to three active emotions as players at the table. Observe them before deciding.
2. Vetoes — Give each emotion one safe veto: ‘Fear will not accept ___. Anger will not accept ___. Sadness will not accept ___.’
3. Clear Board — Mentally remove actions blocked by any safe, reasonable veto. Ignore demands for harm, punishment, or impossible certainty.
4. Choose Survivor — Choose one remaining action that crosses no red line, even if no feeling loves it.
win: Several feelings named one safe veto each, leaving a move that no emotion loved but none had to betray.
supports:
• Separate facts from tone; avoid guessing their intent.
• Separate tone from facts; confirm who will do what.
• Use one concrete example; ask what they understood.
• Name the desired change; ask what they heard.
• Use shorter sentences when tense; lead with the point.

safety:
PAUSE

• Use shorter sentences when tense; lead with the point.

PAUSE

supports:

• Touch the first item; begin with the easiest part.
• Do the easiest useful part; make it visible.

title: PRACTISE THE QUALITY ANONYMOUSLY
goal: Practise one unfamiliar positive quality privately before deciding whether it is 'you'.
steps:
1. Choose Positive — Choose a positive quality that feels “not me.” Do one behaviour that expresses it without announcing the quality or claiming a new identity.
2. Ask Brave — Ask the brave question, make the playful move, accept the compliment, or offer the clear boundary.
3. Let Proof Arrive — Let evidence arrive before identity approval.
win: The behaviour happened without announcing a new identity, letting evidence arrive before self-definition.
supports:
• Do not debate your limit; let guilt pass.
• Delay your answer; decide your limit before answering.
• Repeat without arguing; offer only genuine options.
• Leave their reaction with them; keep the limit simple.
• Leave reactions with them; do not overexplain the limit.

title: POWER THEN, RESOURCES NOW
goal: Compare the resources you had then with the choices and support available now.
steps:
1. Imagine Two Sides — Imagine two sides.
2. Then — On the first side, picture your age, knowledge, money, power, support, and choices then.
3. Picture Today — On the second side, picture the same things today.
4. Find The Change — Notice what gives you more choice now.
5. Use One Resource — Pick one resource you have today and use it in one small action.
win: One present-day resource that did not exist before was used in a small action.
supports:
• Remove one barrier; start physically.
• Reward starting, not finishing; make it visible.
• Lower the first demand; start smaller.
• Set a two-minute timer; restart quickly.
• Begin with the easiest part; skip extra setup.

title: MAKE PROGRESS LEAVE FOOTPRINTS
goal: Make completed units visible so effort cannot disappear from memory.
steps:
1. Choose Marker — Imagine one simple mental marker for each finished unit: a dot, notch, light, or tick.

3. See the Trail — Picture the markers forming a short trail so completed effort stays visible.
win: Only genuinely finished pieces received markers, creating a short trail of evidence behind the work.

• Use a visible cue; choose tiny action.
• Set a two-minute timer; lower the first demand.
• Remove one barrier; do the easiest useful part.

title: LET THE SHAKE BE SMALL
goal: Allow a small safe tremor to complete without clamping down or exaggerating it.
steps:
1. Medically — If medically safe and oriented, permit a small tremor rather than clamping it down.
2. Track Location — Track its location, rhythm, and whether choice remains intact.
3. Let Migrate — Let it stop, continue, or migrate without exaggeration.
4. Let Shake Finish — Ground when the movement ends.
win: The movement could continue, migrate, or stop while orientation and choice remained intact.
supports:
• Rest before deciding; name the emotion.
• Check the facts separately; lower nearby noise.
• Do one steadying action; use plain language.
• Name the feeling plainly; let intensity fall.
• Delay the message; notice body tension.

title: THREE TEMPERATURE FACTS
goal: Read three simple temperature differences instead of interpreting the whole body state.
steps:
1. Check Temperature — Check temperature at three locations: hands, face, and where clothing meets skin.
2. Use Comparative — Use comparative language—cooler, warmer, neutral—rather than guessing degrees.
3. Let Readings — Let the three readings define the body’s current climate.
win: Hands, face, and clothing contact produced a small factual map of warmer, cooler, or neutral.
supports:
• Look around the room; slow your physical pace.
• Feel your feet; notice three colours.
• Notice where your body is supported; touch a stable surface.
• Look around slowly; notice temperature and texture.
• Name three visible objects; feel both feet.

title: SCENT THE RETURN
goal: Pair a safe scent with moments when you are genuinely back in present time.
steps:
1. Choose Safe — Take a mild, distinctive scent that feels safe.
2. Use After — Apply it only after you have really returned to present time and choice.
3. Date Grounding — Pair it with date, place, and one grounding action across several occasions.
4. Test Whether — Later, test whether the scent helps retrieve that state.
win: Date, place, grounding action, and scent were linked only after orientation and choice had returned.
supports:
• Name today's date; keep eyes open.
• Notice room temperature; slow your physical pace.
• Notice temperature and texture; reduce sensory input if needed.
• Name three visible objects; touch a stable surface.
• Keep your eyes on something steady; look around slowly.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Choose Safe — Take a mild, distinctive scent that feels safe.
2. Use After — Apply it only after you have really returned to present time and choice.
3. Date Grounding — Pair it with date, place, and one grounding action across several occasions.
4. Test Whether — Later, test whether the scent helps retrieve that state.

WIN
Date, place, grounding action, and scent were linked only after orientation and choice had returned.

• Name today's date; keep eyes open.
• Notice room temperature; slow your physical pace.
• Notice temperature and texture; reduce sensory input if needed.
• Name three visible objects; touch a stable surface.
• Keep your eyes on something steady; look around slowly.

MIND BEND
A cue retrieves what it was repeatedly paired with. Timing matters more than the pleasantness of the cue.

FORMULA FLOW
Choose Safe → Use After → Date Grounding → Test Whether

SAFETY
PAUSE
Avoid allergens, pregnancy-sensitive scents, substance cues, and public exposure concerns.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MOVE THE VALUE TO A NEW VESSEL
goal: Move the value tied to a loss into a new honest channel without calling it a replacement.
steps:
1. Name Lost — Name what the lost person, role, place, or ability allowed you to express—care, mastery, belonging, beauty, service.
2. Find Different — Find a different, honest channel for a small portion of that value.
3. Start — Begin without treating substitution as replacement.
win: Care, mastery, belonging, beauty, or service found one small new vessel while the original loss stayed acknowledged.
supports:
• Name today's value; use values to choose trade-offs.
• Choose aligned action; act before motivation.
• Name what matters today; check whose goal you are chasing.
• Check whose goal; review what the action costs.
• Use one priority; accept the trade-off.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not rush reconstruction before the loss has been acknowledged.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MAKE THE ORDINARY WORTHY OF FULL CONTACT
goal: Give one ordinary routine full attention as if its usefulness made it worthy.
steps:
1. Choose Routine — Choose one routine act—making tea, bathing, preparing a child’s bag, opening work.
2. Perform — Do it without rushing or secondary media.
3. Craft — Notice craft, dependence, and life supported by the act.
4. Finish Deserved — Finish as if it deserved completion.
win: A simple act was completed without rushing or secondary media, and the life it supported became visible.
supports:
• Ask what failure would cost; use strongest evidence.
• Keep new facts separate; commit once chosen.
• Reduce the options; set a deadline.
• Stop researching after enough evidence; accept one trade-off.
• Ignore imagined regret; choose the option you can support.

safety:

title: CATCH THE MOMENT ‘MINE’ ARRIVES
goal: Catch the extra moment when a thought or sensation changes from 'there' to 'mine'.
steps:
1. Wait Sensation — Wait for a sensation or thought to appear.
2. Catch Ownership — Notice its first instant, then watch for the extra sense of ‘my thought,’ ‘my pain,’ or ‘about me.’ Notice the interval between appearance and possession without trying to change it.
win: Appearance and ownership became two distinguishable moments without needing to remove either one.
supports:
• Reduce commentary; notice the thought, then step back.
• Keep one real task in view; use simple present-tense facts.
• Return to the room; notice where attention goes.
• Keep one task; use present facts.
• Use fewer words; let it pass.
formula_flow: Wait Sensation → Catch Ownership
safety:
PAUSE
Use first-person sensory grounding when self-distance feels destabilising.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: OPEN THREE ENDING ROOMS
goal: Compare three possible endings at the decision point, then choose the one best supported by evidence and values.
steps:
1. Identify Critical — Spot the critical decision point in the dominant future scene.
2. Create Endings — Create three endings by changing the choice there: cautious, courageous, and collaborative.
3. Cost — Notice the cost and value of each.
4. Keep Best — Keep the ending that best fits evidence and values.
win: Cautious, courageous, and collaborative endings showed different costs before one path earned the next move.
supports:
• Pick one value for this decision; accept the trade-off.
• Name what matters today; remove one conflicting commitment.
• Check whose goal you are chasing; remove one conflict.
• Keep meaning practical; choose aligned action.
• Name today's value; protect important time.
formula_flow: Identify Critical → Create Endings → Cost → Keep Best
safety:
PAUSE
Do not imagine unsafe endings merely to increase variety.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: COMMON IS NOT THE SAME AS RIGHT
goal: Judge a social norm by harm, fairness, consent, dignity, and responsibility rather than popularity.
steps:
1. State Social — State the social norm and your chosen criteria—harm, fairness, consent, dignity, responsibility.
2. Evaluate — Check the norm against each criterion without citing popularity.
3. Keep Modify — Keep, modify, or reject it based on the ethical comparison.
win: The norm was kept, changed, or rejected without using 'everyone does it' as evidence.
supports:
• Stop checking their numbers; do one action for your life.
• Notice what you cannot see; return to your own baseline.
• Use your own priorities; compare with your past self.
• Limit social media exposure; name one thing already working.
• Avoid one-person benchmarks; return to your priorities.
formula_flow: State Social → Evaluate → Keep Modify
safety:
PAUSE
Consult affected communities and expertise when personal criteria are incomplete.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: RETURN THE SHAME TO ITS OLD ADDRESS
goal: Keep any repair that truly belongs to you and return inherited contempt or impossible standards to their source.
steps:
1. Identify Whose — Spot whose rule the shame is enforcing and the setting where it was learned.
2. Ask Whether — Check whether you still endorse that standard.
3. Keep Repair — Keep any ethical repair that is truly yours; return contempt, prejudice, or impossible expectation to its source.
win: The old rule was identified, current endorsement was checked, and shame lost the parts that were never ethically yours.
supports:
• Avoid global words like always; prefer repair.
• Separate guilt from responsibility; describe the behaviour, not yourself.
• Keep guilt precise; do not punish yourself for learning.
• Avoid global labels; name the behaviour.
• Recall capability; make repair smaller than self-punishment.
formula_flow: Identify Whose → Ask Whether → Keep Repair
safety:
PAUSE
Seek support when shame is severe, trauma-linked, or tied to self-harm.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: RETURN RECEIPT
goal: Break the delay by doing the smallest workable part and naming the re-entry location.
steps:
1. Open It — Notice the moment you know the first task but keep delaying the start.
2. Begin Now — Do the smallest workable part of the task.
3. Save Place — Identify the specific location and move for re-entry.

title: CHARACTER OUT, FACTS IN
goal: Remove character judgment from the work issue and wait before deciding what the fact requires.
steps:

5. Postpone Move — Wait ten minutes before deciding.
win: One observable fact stayed in view for ten minutes while the threat story lost access to the decision.

title: TURN FEEDBACK INTO ONE ACTION
goal: Turn one feedback point into one visible action and record what changed.
steps:
1. Voice It — Speak a single specific line aloud.
2. Divide Parts — Separate the requested change from the motive you are assuming.
3. Do One — Make one visible first action.
4. Log Win — Name what worked this time.
5. Check Result — Name what moved without retelling the whole exchange.
win: Motive stayed out, the first action happened, and the exchange ended on evidence instead of another explanation.
supports:
• Stay specific; agree one follow-up point.
• Keep it short; state expected change.
• Describe the impact; set follow-up point.
• Ask what got in the way; keep criticism about behaviour.
• Do not soften until unclear; keep the message short.

title: SET THE ANCHOR
goal: Anchor to the environment and bring another person in while the alarm is loud.
steps:
1. Find Room — Fix your eyes on one doorway.
2. Label Alarm — Say, ‘This may be body alarm.’
3. Cool Pace — Slow one movement by half.
4. Shift Body — Press both feet toward the floor.
5. Reach Person — Call one trusted person now.
win: A doorway, your feet, and a slower movement gave you external reference points before you contacted support.
supports:
• Avoid symptom searching; unclench your jaw.
• Look at ordinary objects nearby; wait out the surge.
• Stop body scanning; avoid repeated pulse checking.
• Reduce extra stimulation; seek care for new severe symptoms.
• Keep movements gentle; let breathing stay natural.
formula_flow: Find Room → Label Alarm → Cool Pace → Shift Body → Reach Person
safety:
PAUSE
Keep your eyes open and orient to the room. Stop if symptoms intensify, you feel faint, or a medical problem may be possible. Call Triple Zero (000) for an emergency; otherwise use qualified medical advice. Do not induce or test symptoms.
This is brief self-help, not diagnosis or treatment.

title: HOLD THE PAUSE
goal: Delay the urge decision, move normally, and replace internal checking with a calm human voice.
steps:
1. Label Alarm — Name one sensation you can feel right now.
2. Postpone Move — Set the decision aside for ten minutes.
3. Catch Thought — Say the recurring query in your head.
4. Change Place — Shift into one ordinary movement, such as standing, walking, or getting water.
5. Stay Connected — Reach a calm human voice.
win: Ten minutes were protected from decision-making and ordinary movement led toward live support instead of another internal query.
supports:
• Eat if hungry; delay acting for ten minutes.
• Make access less convenient; remember urges peak and fall.
• Tell someone early; do one incompatible activity.
• Move away from the cue; use your hands.
• Change locations; tell someone if the urge spikes.
formula_flow: Label Alarm → Postpone Move → Catch Thought → Change Place → Stay Connected
safety:
PAUSE
Move away from access, money, apps, substances, traffic, or other hazards. Contact a trusted person or qualified service if the urge feels difficult to manage safely. Call Triple Zero (000) for immediate danger.
This is brief self-help, not treatment or emergency care.

title: SAY THE SENTENCE THAT OPENS HELP
play_time: ACT NOW — MOVE TO LIVE SUPPORT
goal: Stop analysing the frightening experience and say the sentence that gets live help involved.
steps:
1. Stop Interpretation — Stop analysing what the experience means or why it started.
2. Choose Contact Method — Call a trusted person, crisis service, or emergency responder.
3. Read Help Sentence — Say, “My experience feels frightening and I need support now.”
4. Follow Their Direction — Follow instructions that reduce risk and arrange assessment.
5. Keep Line Open — Keep the call or in-person contact active until help continues.
win: A trusted person, crisis service, or emergency responder stayed connected and the next safety instructions came from outside the experience.
supports:
• Have a trusted person stay nearby.
• Lower nearby stimulation.
• Avoid alcohol or recreational drugs.
• Describe the experience without interpreting it.
• Seek professional support today.
formula_flow: Stop Interpretation → Choose Contact Method → Read Help Sentence → Follow Their Direction → Keep Line Open
safety:
PAUSE
IMMEDIATE DANGER OR POSSIBLE MEDICAL EMERGENCY: call Triple Zero (000) now.
24/7 CRISIS SUPPORT: call Lifeline 13 11 14 or text 0477 13 11 14.
Stay with a safe person and follow qualified support. Do not return to ordinary rituals.

title: MARGIN AROUND THE LOOP
goal: Give a recurring question a boundary, complete something outside it, and end this round of the loop.
steps:
1. Voice It — Say the repeated question once, exactly as it keeps returning.
2. Divide Parts — Ask how the signal differs from the intention.
3. Hold Later — Choose the later questions as your restart marker.
4. Take Action — Complete one bounded task outside the loop.
5. Close Loop — End the unfinished mental loop.
win: The question was said once, a later restart marker was chosen, and one bounded task finished outside the loop.
supports:
• Name one action; set a clear stopping point.
• Leave unsolved questions; use a short timer.
• Return to current task; change rooms if possible.
• Limit how long you review it; stop solving the unsolvable.
• Use your hands; stop repeated review.
formula_flow: Voice It → Divide Parts → Hold Later → Take Action → Close Loop
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if this makes you less steady, more distressed, or less able to act safely. Use human, professional, medical, or emergency support when the situation needs more than self-help.
This brief reset is not diagnosis, treatment, or emergency care.

title: KEEP ONE FACT
goal: Make a decision that fits the uncertainty and capacity available, then set a review point.
steps:
1. Set Unclear — Name what is still uncertain.
2. Count Room — Name how much time or capacity you actually have.
3. Delay Action — Wait one beat before choosing.
4. Take Stock — Choose the next review spot and stop there.
win: The choice was made after one pause and uncertainty was contained by a specific future review rather than repeated reopening.
supports:
• Accept a small margin of risk; name what is known.
• Delay reassurance; use a deadline.
• Use a decision deadline; accept small risk.
• Limit checking; stop reopening choices.
• Delay reassurance seeking; leave one question unanswered.
